name: Cuneiform
tagline: The earliest writing system, pressed into wet clay with a reed stylus.

name: Proto-Elamite
tagline: Contemporary with proto-cuneiform, still unread.

name: Old Persian Cuneiform
tagline: A semi-syllabary that borrowed cuneiform's wedges but not its system.

name: Ugaritic
tagline: An alphabet written in wedges — cuneiform's shapes, Canaan's system.

name: Anatolian Hieroglyphs
tagline: An indigenous Anatolian logosyllabary, read boustrophedon.

name: Egyptian Hieroglyphs
tagline: Logo-consonantal, monumental, and the distant ancestor of most letters now in use.

name: Hieratic
tagline: The priestly cursive — hieroglyphs written fast, with a brush on papyrus.

name: Demotic
tagline: The 'popular' script of Late Period Egypt, and the middle band of the Rosetta Stone.

name: Meroitic
tagline: Nubia's own script: Egyptian signs, an African language nobody can yet read.

name: Coptic
tagline: The last stage of Egyptian, written in Greek letters plus six demotic signs.

name: Cretan Hieroglyphs
tagline: Minoan Crete's first script, found mostly on seals, undeciphered.

name: Linear A
tagline: The Minoan administrative script. Readable in sound, unreadable in sense.

name: Linear B
tagline: Greek written five centuries before the Greek alphabet, and forgotten.

name: Cypro-Minoan
tagline: Cyprus's Bronze Age syllabary, adapted from Linear A and still unread.

name: Cypriot Syllabary
tagline: Greek written syllabically for seven centuries, alongside the alphabet.

name: Maya Script
tagline: The only substantially deciphered writing system of the Americas.

name: Isthmian (Epi-Olmec)
tagline: A sparse Mesoamerican corpus, claimed as deciphered and widely doubted.

name: Zapotec
tagline: Monte Albán's monumental script, the earliest writing in Mesoamerica.

name: Aztec (Nahuatl) Writing
tagline: Pictorial codices with rebus name-glyphs, in the Mixteca-Puebla tradition.

name: Indus Script
tagline: Thousands of seals, no long texts, and no agreed reading.

name: Rongorongo
tagline: Twenty-six wooden objects, carved in reverse boustrophedon, unread.

name: Voynich Manuscript Script
tagline: A single illustrated codex in an alphabet used nowhere else.

name: Proto-Sinaitic
tagline: The first alphabet: about forty inscriptions from a turquoise mine, and the ancestor of A.

name: Proto-Canaanite
tagline: The Late Bronze Age stage between the Sinai inscriptions and Phoenician.

name: Phoenician
tagline: Twenty-two consonants, one fixed direction, and the parent of Greek and Aramaic alike.

name: Paleo-Hebrew
tagline: The original Hebrew script, displaced by Aramaic but not quite killed.

name: Samaritan
tagline: The only living descendant of the original Hebrew letterforms.

name: Ancient South Arabian
tagline: The monumental musnad of Saba, and the parent of Ethiopian writing.

name: Ancient North Arabian
region: Northern Arabia and the Syrian desert
tagline: Tens of thousands of desert graffiti in a family of related alphabets.

name: Ge'ez (Ethiopic)
tagline: An abugida invented in fourth-century Aksum, still written every day.

name: Tifinagh
tagline: The Berber script: ancient Libyco-Berber, kept alive by the Tuareg and now official in Morocco.

name: Aramaic
tagline: The most generative script in history: nearly every Middle Eastern and Indian writing system runs through it.

name: Hebrew
tagline: The Aramaic square script, adopted for Hebrew and never given up.

name: Syriac
tagline: Three cursive hands that carried Christianity from Edessa to China.

name: Mandaic
tagline: The script of the Mandaeans, in which every letter is a vowel or a consonant.

name: Palmyrene
tagline: The monumental hand of a caravan city, and the first Semitic script deciphered.

name: Nabataean
tagline: Petra's cursive, which ligatured itself into the Arabic alphabet.

name: Arabic
region: North Africa, the Middle East, South and Southeast Asia
tagline: The second most widely used script on earth, and the most thoroughly cursive.

name: Perso-Arabic
tagline: Arabic plus four letters, and the model for every eastern adaptation.

name: Urdu (Nastaliq)
tagline: Perso-Arabic with retroflexes, set on a diagonal baseline.

name: Thaana
tagline: A Maldivian invention whose consonants are derived from numerals.

name: Hanifi Rohingya
tagline: A modern alphabet built on Arabic forms for a stateless language.

name: Pahlavi
tagline: Middle Persian in Aramaic letters, with Aramaic words read aloud as Persian.

name: Avestan
tagline: A phonetically engineered alphabet, designed to record scripture exactly.

name: Sogdian
tagline: The Silk Road's commercial cursive, and the hinge to Inner Asia.

name: Old Uyghur
tagline: Sogdian turned on its side, and the ancestor of the Mongolian script.

name: Mongolian
tagline: The only major living script written in vertical columns left to right.

name: Manchu
tagline: The Mongolian script with dots and circles, and the language of the Qing court.

name: Old Turkic (Orkhon)
tagline: The runiform script of the Orkhon inscriptions, the oldest Turkic texts.

name: Kharosthi
tagline: Brahmi's right-to-left sibling, the script of Gandharan Buddhism.

name: Greek
region: Greece, Cyprus, and the ancient Mediterranean
tagline: The first script to write vowels as letters in their own right.

name: Old Italic
tagline: The Euboean Greek alphabet, reshaped across pre-Roman Italy.

name: Latin
tagline: The most widely used script in history, by a very wide margin.

name: Runic (Futhark)
tagline: Angular Germanic letters cut for wood and stone, named for 'secret'.

name: Ogham
tagline: Notches cut across the edge of a standing stone, read upwards.

name: Gothic
tagline: Designed by a bishop in the fourth century to translate the Bible.

name: Armenian
tagline: Created in AD 405 by Mesrop Mashtots, and essentially unchanged since.

name: Georgian
tagline: Three successive alphabets for one language, all still legible in Georgia.

name: Glagolitic
tagline: Saint Cyril's original Slavic alphabet, invented for a mission in 863.

name: Cyrillic
region: Eastern Europe, Russia, Central Asia, the Caucasus
tagline: Named for Cyril, but built by his students at Preslav after his death.

name: Old Permic (Abur)
tagline: A fourteenth-century missionary alphabet for Komi, mixing Cyrillic with tamga marks.

name: Deseret
tagline: A phonemic replacement for English spelling, sponsored by Brigham Young.

name: Shavian
tagline: Bernard Shaw left money in his will for a better English alphabet.

name: International Phonetic Alphabet
tagline: One symbol per speech sound, for every language on earth.

name: Braille
tagline: A tactile six-dot cell, devised by a fifteen-year-old in 1824.

name: Brahmi
tagline: The ancestor of 198 scripts, and the first alphabet to organise itself by phonetics.

name: Gupta (Late Brahmi)
tagline: The northern cursive of the Gupta empire, from which most Indian scripts descend.

name: Siddham
tagline: The Buddhist script of the Silk Road, still written by Japanese calligraphers.

name: Sharada
tagline: Kashmir's script, and the root of the Landa commercial hands.

name: Nagari
tagline: The 'urban' script of medieval India, parent of Devanagari and Nandinagari.

name: Devanagari
tagline: The fourth most widely used writing system on earth, in over 120 languages.

name: Gurmukhi
tagline: Standardised by the second Sikh Guru so scripture could be written exactly.

name: Gujarati
tagline: Devanagari with the headline removed, for speed of writing.

name: Bengali–Assamese
tagline: The fifth most used script in the world, shared by two national languages.

name: Odia
tagline: Rounded tops, because a straight stylus stroke splits a palm leaf.

name: Tibetan
tagline: Commissioned by a seventh-century emperor, and famously conservative in spelling.

name: ʼPhags-pa
tagline: A universal script for the Mongol empire, designed by a Tibetan lama in 1269.

name: Kadamba
tagline: Southern Brahmi in the Deccan, parent of Kannada and Telugu.

name: Kannada
tagline: The rounded Deccan hand, for one of India's oldest literary languages.

name: Telugu
tagline: Distinctive tick-marked letters for the most spoken Dravidian language.

name: Pallava (Grantha)
region: Tamil Nadu and maritime Southeast Asia
tagline: The script Tamil merchants carried to Southeast Asia, seeding a dozen alphabets.

name: Tamil
region: Tamil Nadu, Sri Lanka, Singapore, Malaysia
tagline: The simplest Brahmic inventory, because Tamil needs no aspirates.

name: Malayalam
tagline: Grantha's fullest development, with the largest letter inventory in India.

name: Sinhala
tagline: Sri Lanka's rounded script, with prenasalised consonants unique in the family.

name: Khmer
tagline: The oldest dated inscription in Southeast Asia, and the parent of Thai and Lao.

name: Thai
tagline: Attributed to King Ram Khamhaeng in 1283, and tonally ingenious.

name: Lao
tagline: Thai's sibling, deliberately simplified by twentieth-century reform.

name: Mon–Burmese
tagline: Circles, because a straight line splits a palm leaf.

name: Kawi (Old Javanese)
region: Java, Bali, and maritime Southeast Asia
tagline: The maritime Southeast Asian script from which a dozen island alphabets grew.

name: Balinese
tagline: Still cut into palm-leaf lontar manuscripts by Balinese scribes.

name: Javanese (Hanacaraka)
tagline: Named for the first four letters of a sentence about two quarrelling messengers.

name: Baybayin
tagline: Widely literate at Spanish contact, then almost completely lost.

name: Cham
tagline: The Champa kingdom's script, and the oldest Indic script in Southeast Asia.

name: Ol Chiki
tagline: Designed in 1925 so Santali would not have to be written in anyone else's alphabet.

name: Canadian Aboriginal Syllabics
tagline: The vowel is written by rotating the consonant — unique among the world's scripts.

name: Pollard (Miao)
tagline: A Canadian syllabics-inspired script for the Hmong of Guizhou.

name: Oracle Bone Script
tagline: Divination questions carved on ox scapulae and turtle plastrons.

name: Seal Script
tagline: Standardised by the Qin after unification, and still cut into seals today.

name: Chinese Characters (Traditional)
region: Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau, and diaspora
tagline: The only one of the four original inventions of writing still in continuous use.

name: Chinese Characters (Simplified)
tagline: A 1956 state reform that reduced stroke counts for mass literacy.

name: Kanji
tagline: Chinese characters adapted to a completely unrelated language.

name: Man'yōgana
tagline: Chinese characters used purely for sound, and the raw material of kana.

name: Hiragana
tagline: The cursive 'women's hand' that became Japan's default syllabary.

name: Katakana
tagline: Fragments of characters, invented by monks annotating sutras.

name: Hanja
tagline: Chinese characters in Korea, now largely retired in favour of Hangul.

name: Chữ Nôm
tagline: Over ten thousand new characters for Vietnamese, abandoned in a generation.

name: Sawndip
tagline: Zhuang written in adapted Chinese characters for over a millennium, unofficially.

name: Nüshu
tagline: A syllabary used only by women, in one county, for four centuries.

name: Bopomofo (Zhuyin)
tagline: A phonetic notation built from fragments of ancient characters.

name: Khitan Large Script
tagline: Commissioned in 920 by an emperor who wanted his own writing.

name: Khitan Small Script
tagline: Phonetic elements assembled into square blocks — five centuries before Hangul.

name: Jurchen
tagline: The Jin dynasty's script, modelled on Khitan and Chinese.

name: Tangut
tagline: Nearly six thousand brand-new characters, decreed into existence in 1036.

name: Yi (Nuosu)
tagline: A classical logographic script, reformed in 1974 into a 756-sign syllabary.

name: Dongba
tagline: The world's only pictographic system still used by living priests.

name: Hangul
tagline: The one script whose inventor explained his reasoning, and shaped the letters like the mouth.

name: Cherokee
region: Oklahoma and North Carolina, United States
tagline: Invented by an illiterate silversmith who reasoned out how writing must work.

name: Vai
tagline: A West African syllabary said to have been revealed in a dream.

name: N'Ko
tagline: Created in 1949 for the Manding languages, and spread by grassroots literacy campaigns.

name: Adlam
tagline: Invented by two teenage brothers in 1989, and now on Android keyboards.

name: Bamum
tagline: A king's script, revised six times in twenty years from pictographs to a syllabary.

name: Pahawh Hmong
region: Laos, Vietnam, and the Hmong diaspora
tagline: A messianic script that writes the rime before the onset.

name: Mwangwego
tagline: A Malawian abugida designed in 1979, taught by its inventor for decades.

name: Osage
tagline: A twenty-first-century alphabet, created so a language could be revived on its own terms.

name: Afaka
tagline: A syllabary for a Surinamese creole, said to have come in a dream in 1908.

name: Shorthand (Pitman & Gregg)
tagline: Phonetic systems built for speed, and an influence on two continents' scripts.

name: Tocharian
tagline: The slanting Brahmi of the Silk Road, recording two extinct Indo-European languages spoken in what is now Xinjiang.

name: Meitei Mayek
tagline: Every letter is named after a part of the human body, and the whole script was brought back from disuse by act of legislature.

name: Modi
tagline: A cursive shorthand for Devanagari, designed so a clerk need not lift the pen to re-ink it.

name: Tai Tham (Lanna)
region: Northern Thailand, Laos, Shan State, Sipsong Panna
tagline: The palm-leaf script of Lan Na, whose rounded letters exist because a straight stroke tears a leaf along its fibres.

name: Grantha
tagline: A classical South Indian Brahmic script primarily used to write Sanskrit and the ancestor of the modern Malayalam script.

name: Tigalari (Tulu)
region: Tulu Nadu and Malnad regions of Karnataka, India
tagline: Tigalari is a Southern Brahmic script historically used in coastal Karnataka to write Sanskrit, Tulu, and Kannada.

name: Nandinagari
region: Southern India (Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu)
tagline: Nandinagari is a historical Brahmic script that served as the official script of the Vijayanagara Empire for writing Sanskrit in southern India.

name: Kaithi
region: Northern and Eastern India (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand)
tagline: Kaithi was the primary administrative and legal script of North India for centuries before being displaced by Devanagari under British rule.

name: Sylheti Nagri
tagline: An Indic script uniquely adapted by Bengali Muslims to write Islamic poetry and literature in the Sylhet region.

name: Takri
region: Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Punjab, and Uttarakhand, India
tagline: A Brahmic abugida formerly used across the western Himalayas for administrative and literary records before being replaced by Devanagari.

name: Multani
region: Multan region of Punjab and northern Sindh, Pakistan
tagline: A mercantile script of the Punjab that briefly flourished as a literary medium before being replaced by the Arabic script.

name: Khojki
region: Sindh, Punjab, and Gujarat (present-day Pakistan and India)
tagline: Khojki is a Landa-derived script historically used by the Nizari Ismaili community of South Asia to record their sacred devotional poetry.

name: Khudawadi
tagline: A Landa-based mercantile script standardized in the 19th century for the Sindhi language before being eclipsed by the Perso-Arabic script.

name: Chakma
region: Chittagong Hill Tracts (Bangladesh) and Northeastern India (Mizoram, Tripura, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh)
tagline: An indigenous Brahmic abugida of Bangladesh and Northeast India, notable for its inherent long 'ā' vowel and recent digital revitalization.

name: Lepcha
tagline: An abugida derived from Tibetan that features unique superposed final consonants due to a historical 90-degree rotation in its writing direction.

name: Limbu
tagline: The Limbu script is a Brahmic abugida invented in the 18th century to write the Limbu language and preserve its oral traditions.

name: Tirhuta
region: Mithila region (Bihar, India and southern Nepal)
tagline: An ancient Brahmic abugida historically used to write Maithili and Sanskrit in the Mithila region, now largely replaced by Devanagari.

name: Saurashtra
tagline: A Brahmic script developed in the late 19th century to write the Saurashtra language in Tamil Nadu.

name: Ranjana
tagline: An ornate Brahmic script used for centuries to write Sanskrit and Newar, renowned for its calligraphic beauty and use in Buddhist texts.

name: Soyombo
tagline: An intricate 17th-century Mongolian abugida created by Zanabazar for Buddhist translations, whose special symbol became Mongolia's national emblem.

name: Zanabazar Square
tagline: A horizontal square script created by Zanabazar to write Mongolian, Tibetan, and Sanskrit.

name: Marchen
tagline: The Marchen script is a Tibetan-derived abugida historically used by the Bön religion to write the extinct Zhang-Zhung language of western Tibet.

name: Tai Le
tagline: A Brahmic script used by the Tai Nüa people that underwent significant modern reforms to improve its phonetic accuracy.

name: New Tai Lue
tagline: A 1950s Chinese government simplification of the traditional Tai Tham script designed to boost literacy among the Tai Lü people.

name: Tai Viet
region: Northwestern Vietnam, northern Laos, central Thailand
tagline: The Tai Viet script is a Brahmic abugida used by the Tai Dam and other Tai peoples in Vietnam, notable for lacking inherent vowels.

name: Buhid
tagline: An indigenous Brahmic abugida of the Philippines, still actively used by the Mangyan people of Mindoro to write poetry and songs on bamboo.

name: Hanunoo
tagline: An indigenous Philippine script famous for being written vertically upward on bamboo to record traditional poetry.

name: Tagbanwa
tagline: Tagbanwa is an endangered indigenous Philippine script traditionally written bottom-to-top on bamboo but read horizontally.

name: Rejang
tagline: An indigenous Brahmic script of Sumatra traditionally incised on bamboo and buffalo horn.

name: Lontara (Buginese)
region: South Sulawesi and West Sulawesi, Indonesia
tagline: Lontara is a Brahmic script of South Sulawesi, historically written on rolled palm leaves and used for Buginese genealogies and daily registers.

name: Batak
tagline: An abugida from Sumatra historically used by magician-priests for magical texts and divinatory books.

name: Sundanese
tagline: The Sundanese script is a revived indigenous writing system of West Java, Indonesia, based on a 14th-century script.

name: Serbian Cyrillic
tagline: A highly phonetic Cyrillic alphabet reformed in 1818 by Vuk Karadžić to perfectly match the spoken Serbian language.

name: Lisu (Fraser)
tagline: An artificial abugida created in 1915 using rotated Latin uppercase letters to write the Lisu language.

name: Mundari Bani
tagline: Mundari Bani is a 20th-century alphabetic script created to write the Austroasiatic Mundari language of eastern India.

name: Tangsa
region: Arunachal Pradesh, India and Sagaing Region, Myanmar
tagline: An original alphabet created in 1990 for the Tangsa language, notable for having distinct vowel letters for each of the language's four tones.

name: Wancho
tagline: An independent alphabet created in the 21st century to preserve the Wancho language and culture.

name: Medefaidrin
tagline: Medefaidrin is a constructed script created in 1930s Nigeria to write a Christian "spirit language" rooted in glossolalia.
